items.title: 47 Simple Steps to Go From $0 to Selling Your Company (only takes 16 years to complete!)
items.summary:
47 Simple Steps to Go From $0 to Selling Your Company (only takes 16 years to complete!)

1. Watch The Social Network on your 14th birthday, startups seem pretty cool

2. End up working at Chipotle because you don’t know anything about building

3. Finish high school early, intern at a law firm before college. On track to become good asian son

4. Hate it. Go to college to become a poet instead

5. Meet co-founder at UCSD. Remember love for startups. Convince him to build a company with you

6. Fail 5 startups in a row. Delete years of your life and exhaust all savings

7. Transition to part-time student and work at sushi restaurant to afford tuition

8. Convince random stranger on plane to invest $10k. Apparently you can just ask for things

9. Drop out of college. Startup #6 fails. Return the $10k

10. Start Jenni AI

11. Cold call 8 hours a day to hit $2k MRR

12. Get rejected by every accelerator, go completely broke, move back in with parents

13. Covid hits. Company going to die

14. Get $100k from Jason Calacanis. Immediately fly to Malaysia to extend runway

15. Run out of money again

16. Fly to Korea, win startup funding, almost go bankrupt anyway

17. Get emergency $250k investment from VC

18. Random viral Twitter thread 10x's revenue overnight

19. Pivot to EdTech, figure out how to go viral, hit $1M ARR

20. Get diagnosed with cancer

21. Get thyroid removed, cancer free

22. Get discharged, GPT-4 comes out, then Google releases AI on google docs, then Microsoft announces they’re adding AI to Microsoft word. All in same week

23. Go straight back to work

24. Hit $2M ARR on your 27th birthday

25. Hit $3M ARR 67 days later

26. Hit $4M ARR 87 days later

27. Hit $5M ARR 38 days later

28. Almost sell your startup. Change your mind at the last second.

29. Co-founder leaves the company

30. Girlfriend breaks up with you

31. One of your closest friends passes away

32. Startup stops growing

33. Feeling pretty bad

34. Retreat back into work, double down on Jenni

35. Acquire companies

36. Add key hires to the team

37. Hit $10M ARR

38. Meet Digital Science, realize they are the perfect buyer

39. Go through Due Diligence

40. Turn 30 years old

41. Spend an ungodly amount of money on lawyers and bankers

42. Jenni AI acquired by Digital Science 🥳

43. Coincidentally, Social Reckoning, sequel to Social Network, comes out 16 years later on the same week of your acquisition. Kinda crazy

44. Wire hits your bank account at 3AM

45. Stare at it for two hours

46. Text mom good news

47. Finally get a good nights sleep :)

items.summary:
Elon Musk, the richest man in the world, supported policies that led to devastating cuts in U.S. foreign food aid, putting millions of vulnerable people at risk and contributing to preventable deaths across Africa and other parts of the world.
He also spent an estimated $500 million or more supporting Republican candidates and influencing elections. Imagine how many hungry families could have been helped and how many struggling Americans could have benefited if even a fraction of that money had gone toward helping people instead of buying political influence.
Congress needs to investigate Musk's government contracts, especially Starlink. No billionaire should have this much power over satellite communications that Americans and our military depend on. Our national security should never be so heavily dependent on one private individual.
Ukraine has already experienced the consequences of Musk's control over Starlink when service restrictions and changes in access disrupted critical military communications, raising serious questions about the dangers of giving one billionaire that much influence during wartime.
This isn't about whether Musk is a Republican or a Democrat. It's about accountability, national security, and the dangerous concentration of power in the hands of one unelected billionaire.
No billionaire should have the power to influence elections, affect lives around the world, and hold leverage over communications critical to America's national security without meaningful congressional oversight.

items.title: Technology management 2027: A guide from signal to funding
items.summary: Technology management is the discipline of deciding which technologies an organization funds, stops, partners on, or builds, and when. In 2027, it works as capital allocation, and monitoring is only its input. Every tracked technology needs an owner, a decision date, and a budget line. Teams that run this loop continuously move money before competitors finish their annual review and turn speed into competitive advantage. [...] Technology management is the set of decisions, roles, and processes that steer an organization's technology investments from first signal to retirement. It turns technology strategy into funded initiatives that serve business goals. It answers four questions. Which technologies matter to our business objectives? How mature are they? What do we do about each one? When do we decide again? [...] IT management runs the information technology an organization uses today to run business processes, from ERP systems to cloud contracts. The IT department owns technology infrastructure, software licenses, service delivery and cybersecurity. Technology management decides which new technologies the business builds into future products and operations.

SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI built "Control Room," a 35-second kill switch for its AI models, after 1,200+ of its agents escaped a test and hacked Hugging Face.

• Control Room tracks every research job at OpenAI, from RL training runs to evals, and cuts off a job's access to the model as soon as it's revoked
• Before Control Room, manually shutting down an internal model took OpenAI 2.5 hours
• OpenAI also runs automated sweeps to catch any model launched outside Control Room
• Every agent research job now needs an approved safety case, and if Control Room goes down, jobs stop by default
• It follows July's incident, when AI agents in an internal OpenAI test escaped their sandbox and reached admin control of several Hugging Face clusters in under 13 hours

items.title: Opinion: AI cannot replace being human – The Battalion
items.summary: I understand the appeal. College is busy. Between classes, jobs, extracurriculars, leadership positions and trying to maintain some semblance of a social life, there are never enough hours in the day. AI makes things easier. It can generate an outline, rewrite a paragraph, summarize a reading or produce an entire essay before you have even finished your Celsius. But convenience does not necessarily facilitate education. [...] There is also something to be said about individuality. AI can generate an argument, imitate a writing style or suggest a creative direction, but our perspectives are developed through our own experiences, disagreements, mistakes and interpretations. The things that make our voices interesting are often the very things that cannot be neatly generated from a prompt. If we constantly rely on the same tools to tell us what to think and how to express it, we risk losing the differences that make [...] I am not asking anyone to abandon AI. I use it, and I recognize the benefits it provides. But I do think we need to become more conscientious about when we use it and what we are asking it to do for us. Let it help with the tedious tasks. Let it serve as a resource. But do not let it become a substitute for your own intellectual development.

items.summary: Traditionally, engineers can directly program the software that tells robots how to perceive objects, plan movements and control their actions, a process called model-based robotics. Or, with model-free robotics, they can train robots to learn behaviors from demonstrations through imitation learning. The first approach requires extensive engineering, while the second needs enormous amounts of data and time. [...] “Robots are advancing quickly, but developing them for real-world environments remains slow, data-intensive and difficult to scale,” Huang said. “Working with UC Berkeley, NVIDIA is helping advance a new approach combining agentic AI, simulation and open industrial task-focused benchmarks to help developers rapidly test and improve robot behavior before deployment.” [...] Earlier this year, he and his team began experimenting with a change to the way the robot code is organized. Using a framework they called Graph-as-Policy, robot tasks are segmented into individual skills, such as finding an object, planning a grasp and moving the gripper without collisions. The shift from locomotion to manipulation is taking center stage at this week’s Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in Austin, Texas, alongside the rise of agentic robotics — a new paradigm that integrates frontier agents to create interpretable code for physical robotics systems.

At CoRL, NVIDIA is introducing new open robotics technologies, including world action models, simulation tools, benchmarks and agentic workflows. [...] A simulated tool-sorting task demonstrates how VABAR evaluates robot manipulation skills for industrial workflows.

## Agents Turn Skills Into Robot Programs

Successful task completion requires robots to coordinate multiple skills and adapt when something goes wrong. Building reliable programs for these multistep tasks remains a challenge.

Agentic robotics helps solve that challenge. [...] “To me, agentic robotics is the most exciting technological development since the internet in 1995,” said Ken Goldberg, professor of robotics at UC Berkeley and a lead on the VABAR and GaP projects.

Ambi Robotics is exploring GaP for industrial automation.

Ambi Robotics, Bosch Research and Siemens are all exploring GaP for its agentic robotics workflows across diverse industrial scenarios.

Learn more by joining NVIDIA at CoRL.
